newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO ministers want war crimes police in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: NATO ministers want war crimes police in Bosnia.

text.p: NATO defence ministers want a new international police force to hunt down accused war crimes fugitives in Bosnia and that force would have to be protected by peacekeeping troops there, U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said on Wednesday.

But other U.S. and NATO officials also cautioned at the windup of a two-day defence ministers meeting that the ministers were divided on how a police force might be set up and who would provide members to arrest fugitives and turn them over for prosecution by a war crimes tribunal in The Hague.

"They (ministers) agreed that locating and arresting the criminals is a mission for a police force," Perry told a news conference when asked about a U.S. push for a new police force to settle the explosive war crimes issue.

"There was strong agreement among all of the ministers that spoke on the subject that we cannot turn our backs on the problem, that bringing these indicted war criminals to justice is an important mission -- but is not an SFOR mission," he said.

Perry referred to alliance refusal to allow troops in a new NATO-led 31,000-member military stabilisation force (SFOR) to take on police duties of arrest despite international pressure to hunt down dozens of people indicted by the U.N. criminal tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, based in The Hague.
Perry conceded that he and other NATO officials worried "that if a police force were out operating and arresting criminals, this could create a civil disturbance".
"And SFOR would have to deal with that disturbance," he added.
U.S. and NATO officials said earlier on Wednesday that there was broad agreement among ministers that a police force was needed, but there was disagreement on how to handle it.
But a senior U.S. defence official, who asked not to be identified, added: "There isn't yet a specific plan on how to march forward."
The comments came after Perry held morning meetings with French Defence Minister Charles Millon and then the defence ministers of the Netherlands, Norway and Denmark.

The U.S. official told reporters a police force could operate either directly under the so-called war crimes tribunal in The Hague or under the auspices of the European Union or the Organisation on Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
"What the defence ministers are looking for now is what you would call it, who would run it, how it would be organised, who would contribute to it," the official added.

NATO officials cautioned privately that no firm agreement on a police force had been reached, saying all alliance countries were worried about possible retaliation against their troops in Bosnia as well as civilian aid workers.

Former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his former military chief Ratko Mladic -- among those indicted by The Hague tribunal -- enjoy huge popularity among fellow Bosnian Serbs. NATO fears angry crowds would take to the streets if they were arrested.
"The danger is that the Bosnian Serbs, Moslems or Croats would seize hostages or take other retaliatory action against any westerner they find," one NATO official told Reuters.

But Carl Bildt, the international community's representative in charge of overseeing civilian reconstruction in Bosnia, has warned that failure to tackle the war crimes issue would prevent any real reconciliation in that country.

"Refugees will not return and municipal elections are unlikely to be free and fair while these guys (accused war criminals) are still out there," another NATO official conceded privately on Wednesday.

The U.S. official said there was deep concern that only seven out of about 80 suspected war criminals had been captured in the past year and there was broad agreement that those indicted should be captured and tried under the Dayton peace accords.

The official said Millon and Perry met for about 35 minutes and also discussed but reached no agreement on a rift between Washington and Paris over a U.S. refusal to bow to a French demand that the United States turn over command of NATO forces in southern Europe to a European officer.

The job is traditionally held by an American officer and the United States says it should remain that way because the preponderance of allied forces in the region, uncluding the U.S. Sixth Fleet, are American.
